sections.html:
Boeseman's rainbowfish, Melanotaenia boesemani, is a rainbowfish from Indonesia, known only from the Ajamaru lakes and nearby Lakes Hain and Aitinjo. One of the most popular rainbowfish in the hobby, it is almost always sold as farmed stock from the Far East and Eastern Europe. The species is rare in nature and on the IUCN red list, and collection of breeding stock for the trade has had a massively detrimental effect on it. The drab juveniles usually offered for sale can take over 12 months to colour up.

  • Max size: 110 mm SL (4 in)
  • Aquarium size: 120 × 30 cm (48 × 12 in)
  • Temperature: 27–30°C (81–86°F)
  • pH: 7.0–8.0
  • Hardness: 10–20 dGH

Melanotaenia boesemani has the classic rainbowfish profile with a pointed snout, deep-bodied profile, and large, distinct scales. Males grow to 10 cm and display an iridescent blue front half and orange back half. Females are less colorful, have a slimmer body, and tend to stay around 8 cm long.

They are currently endangered in the wild, so the Boeseman's rainbowfish sold in the aquarium hobby are all captive-bred.

Depending on the water temperature, they live about 5–8 years on average, although some hobbyists have reportedly kept them alive for up to 13–15 years.
The rainbowfish seen at pet stores are usually 5 cm juveniles that look washed out and barely resemble the adults. It can take up to a year of good care and high-quality foods for them to color up.
Indonesia.

Has a very limited natural range, being known only from an area of three lakes known as Ajamaru, in the remote Vogelkop Peninsula of Irian Jaya, and from nearby Lakes Hain and Aitinjo. The rainbows tend to congregate in the clear shallows of the lakes, where aquatic vegetation grows very densely. The lakes are characterised by hard, alkaline water (pH 8.0-9.0), although the fish are also found in some surrounding tributaries with wildly different water chemistry (pH 6.0-6.5).
This species is found in mountain lakes and tributaries in West Papua, Indonesia, and usually dwells in shallower areas where lots of vegetation grows.
An active species requiring an aquarium measuring at least 120 × 30 × 30 cm (48 × 12 × 12 in), about 108 litres (29 US gal).

A tank at least 120 cm in length is recommended once they are fully grown, as they like to swim back and forth along the whole length of the aquarium. They stay in the middle to upper half of the water column, so keep a tight lid on the tank.

This species, like most rainbows, looks most at home in a planted aquarium. Provide areas of dense vegetation, along with some open areas for swimming. Other decor is not particularly important. The choice of plants should reflect the slightly hard, alkaline conditions preferred by the fish. Filtration and tank maintenance should be very efficient to encourage the male fish to develop their spectacular colouration.

• Temperature: 27–30°C (81–86°F). Strictly a tropical species.
  • pH: 7.0-8.0. It will not do well in soft, acidic conditions.
  • Hardness: 10-20 dGH

Boesemani rainbowfish are very hardy and tolerate a broad range of water parameters.

  • Temperature: 24–28°C. They can go warmer, but higher temperatures tend to shorten their lifespan.
  • pH: 6–8, although they originate from mildly alkaline water.
  • Hardness: 8–20 dGH. If tap water is softer, consider a mineral supplement.
A densely planted tank with areas of open space for swimming is appreciated.
Unfussy and will accept most dried, frozen and live foods. Regular feedings of the latter will help to ensure the fish exhibit their best colours.

These omnivores are not picky and will eat anything dropped in the tank, but prefer meatier foods. Provide a variety of dry, frozen, and live foods. Rainbowfish have proportionally small mouths, so feed appropriately sized foods such as krill flakes, frozen or freeze-dried bloodworms, daphnia, and brine shrimp.

Very peaceful, but can disturb smaller or slow-moving fish with its rapid movements and relatively large size. Good tankmates include other similarly-sized rainbowfish, characins, danios, barbs, and catfish such as Corydoras. It can also be kept with many species of Rift Lake cichlid, due to its water requirements. Boeseman's rainbowfish can be quite skittish and do far better when kept in a shoal of at least 6-8, preferably more. The males will also be encouraged to display their best colours in the company of conspecifics. Obviously a suitably-sized aquarium would be required for a very large group.

As a schooling fish, keep six or more of the same species, ideally with slightly more females than males so the males display their best colors. Because of their high activity level, keep them with other fast swimmers of comparable size, such as other rainbowfish, loaches, barbs, peaceful catfish, gouramis, danios, and medium-sized livebearers. They will eat cherry shrimp, baby fish, and anything else that fits in their mouths.
Mature males are larger and exhibit brighter colouration than females. They also develop a much deeper body than females as they grow.
Males show an iridescent blue front half and orange back half. Females are less colorful, slimmer, and smaller (about 8 cm).

As with other members of the genus, this is not a difficult species to breed, being an egg scatterer, although the fry can prove somewhat tricky to raise. The breeding aquarium should be at least 30" (about 76 cm) long, and contain slightly hard, alkaline water with a pH of around 7.5 and a temperature of 26.5–29°C (80–84°F). A small air-powered filter will provide sufficient oxygenation and flow. The tank should be filled with fine-leaved plants such as java moss, or nylon spawning mops. No substrate is necessary.

The adult fish are best conditioned in a group in a separate aquarium, with plenty of live and frozen foods. As the fish come into condition, the females will appear noticeably plumper, and males will display to each other almost constantly. Select the fattest, best-coloured pair for spawning and introduce them to the spawning tank. A small raise in temperature can often induce spawning. The pair will spawn for a period of several weeks, laying batches of eggs each day. These are attached to surfaces by a small thread.

Although the adults tend not to eat the spawn, it's easier to raise the fry in a separate aquarium, so it is recommended to check the plants or mops regularly and remove any eggs found to a raising tank containing water from the spawning tank. The eggs hatch in 7-12 days, depending on temperature, and the tiny fry initially require infusoria-type food, before graduating onto free swimming foods, such as brine shrimp nauplii, after a week or so. Sinking foods are unsuitable as the fry tend to stay very close to the water surface.

Boesemanis are one of the easier rainbowfish to spawn, but the tiny fry can be difficult to raise. Condition males and females with heavier feedings. Set up a spawning tank with slightly alkaline pH, a warmer temperature, and a sponge filter, and add the adults with a spawning mop. The male develops a white stripe on his head and performs a shimmying dance to attract a female. Each day they release a small batch of eggs; after 7–10 days, remove either the parents or the eggs to prevent predation.

Feed newborns 3–5 times a day with powdered fry food, vinegar eels, infusoria, and other tiny foods, and keep the water clean with small, frequent water changes. Later move them to baby brine shrimp. The grow-out time is longer than in many other fish.

This uniquely-patterned species is one of the most popular rainbowfish in the hobby and can be found swimming in most dealers' tanks. However, virtually all these fish are mass-produced on fish farms in the Far East and Eastern Europe. M. boesemani is actually quite rare in nature, and is on the IUCN red list of endangered species. Unfortunately this is one species on which the aquarium trade has had a massively detrimental effect, with an estimated one million fish a year being collected to provide breeding stock for the trade.

Adult specimens are rarely seen, and it's the much drabber juvenile fish that are almost always offered for sale. However, with some patience (even on a good diet, full colour development can take over 12 months), you will be rewarded with what is surely one of the most stunning tropical freshwater species available in the hobby.
